opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think I was never the strongest one in that class. When you're in a competition class, you're surrounded by people who are just ridiculously talented. Some of them could see the trick in a problem in thirty seconds, while I'd still be drawing diagrams and trying different approaches. Early on that was pretty humbling, and for a while I measured myself against them very directly, by rankings, by who got into the provincial team, who made it further.

Looking back, though, I think my difference was less about raw talent and more about temperament. A lot of my classmates were incredibly focused on one track. They knew they wanted to win the medal, go to a top university through the competition route, and they optimized for that very cleanly. I was a bit more scattered. I was curious about a lot of things outside the syllabus: reading random stuff, tinkering with computers, wondering why things worked rather than just how to solve them fast. In the short term that probably cost me some points. In the long term it shaped how I approach problems.

The other thing I noticed is that the competition environment trains you to think there's always a correct answer and a clear scoreboard. Many of my classmates were excellent in that world. When we went out into research, industry, and startups, the problems became much more open-ended. There's no answer key, and sometimes you don't even know whether you're asking the right question. I found I was relatively comfortable in that ambiguity, maybe because I was never the person who won purely on speed or precision.

So I wouldn't say I was better or worse. We were good at different games. And honestly, I'm still very grateful to that group. Being around people that sharp set my bar early. It taught me what real excellence looks like, and also that you don't have to be the best in the room to find your own path.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I was the most talented one in that room, and I knew it pretty early. In the competition class there were always a couple of kids who could look at a problem and just see the answer. I wasn't like that. I had to work at it, and sometimes I'd spend a whole evening on something that one of them finished in twenty minutes.

But looking back, I think that was actually useful for me. Because I couldn't rely on raw speed, I got into the habit of asking why something worked instead of just getting it to work. I'd go back over problems I'd already solved and try to understand them from a different angle. That habit mattered more later than any single contest result.

The other thing is, a lot of my classmates were extremely focused on the competitions themselves. They optimized for the medal. I was interested in the competitions, but I was also curious about things outside them, and that sometimes made me look less serious. In hindsight, I think that curiosity is what led me to where I am now. Some of the most gifted people I knew back then ended up on very different paths, and plenty of them are doing well. So I don't think of it as a ranking. We just had different strengths, and mine took a bit longer to show up.

In a competition class, it’s easy to compare yourself with everyone else because you’re all working on the same problems and looking at the same scores. But that’s a pretty narrow measure. Looking back, I’d be more interested in how each of us found something we wanted to pursue. I can appreciate what my classmates do well without treating their progress as a judgment on my own.

When you’re in a competition class, you’re surrounded by people who learn very quickly, and that makes you aware of your own limitations. I could work hard and keep up, but there were classmates whose intuition really impressed me. Looking back, though, I’m less interested in ranking us. We’ve taken different paths, and being good at competitions is only one part of what shapes a person’s life.
